extracted.intended_audience: direct-mail marketers, list brokers, marketing managers, and publishers seeking targeted mailing lists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, selecting, and evaluating mailing lists and direct-mail campaigns that minimize 'junk mail' and maximize relevance and response by precisely targeting prospects and maintaining list quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing and personal relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mail that is addressed by name and is relevant to the recipient's professional or personal needs is perceived as more useful and less like junk mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: professional prepublication notices, catalogs or letters that refer to the recipient's specific interests. Anti-pattern: generic 'Resident' or 'Occupant' addressing that delivers irrelevant offers and increases annoyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source and provenance of list data
rubrics_metrics.description: Mailing lists are compiled from a variety of sources—public records, telephone directories, motor vehicle registries, organization rosters, membership registries, convention rosters, responses to ads or questionnaires, and purchased or rented lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose list sources appropriate to the campaign objective; public-record lists (e.g., Polk, Donnelley) differ from membership or subscriber lists in coverage and suitability. Understand how names were obtained before using them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral qualification (response history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists that include people who have already shown willingness to buy, donate, or subscribe (respondents) are higher-quality prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer lists of individuals who have demonstrated relevant behavior (purchases, subscriptions, donations) rather than cold name/address lists to increase response and reduce waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of targeting (avoid mistargeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of direct mail depends on accurately targeting those prospects who will find the mailing meaningful; mistargeted mail is 'junk mail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in selection criteria and customized lists so that fewer pieces are mailed to uninterested recipients. The more precise the targeting, the less overall mail needed and the higher per-piece value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialized/customized lists (subject-matter match)
rubrics_metrics.description: Customized lists built from domain-specific data (e.g., ISI publication data) can identify narrowly defined professional audiences (researchers currently publishing in a specialty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For highly specialized products (laboratory reagents, niche software), use publication- or profession-based lists that reflect current activity rather than broad membership rosters or course catalogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and psychographic segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilers infer demographics (sex, ethnic group, dwelling type, income) and psychographics (life-style segments) from names, addresses, vehicle data, and overlays with census data to characterize small areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic overlays and psychographic segments when product appeal correlates with such traits; label this information 'demographics' or 'psycho-graphics' depending on depth. Beware of inference errors and privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic granularity and targeting resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists and overlays can characterize geographic areas as small as a few hundred housing units (example: 275 housing units) to target at a fine-grained level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select geographic granularity appropriate to campaign goals (local seminars vs national product launches) and use zip-code or country selection to avoid market/currency problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: List hygiene: duplicate suppression and deduplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated suppression of duplicates caused by authors publishing more than once or other causes prevents redundant mailings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use database features to remove duplicates before printing labels; this reduces postage/material waste and recipient irritation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular updating and re-selection of profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists and selection criteria should be periodically reevaluated and profiles updated to reflect changing needs and new publications or behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer periodic opportunities to refresh selection criteria; maintain a schedule (e.g., weekly generation of new label batches) appropriate to the pace of change in the target population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening and restricting list access
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppliers may screen prospective users and limit list availability to organizations judged to have 'something worthwhile' for the list subjects; screening guards against unauthorized or harmful use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement or require vetting policies to protect list subjects and preserve list integrity; monitor for illicit or fictitious name use as a sign of misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price vs accuracy tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Customized, high-accuracy lists cost more per name (examples: $.35–$.50 per label) but may be worth the premium because they reduce wasted mail and improve response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh list cost against expected reduction in material/postage waste and improved conversion; higher precision justifies higher per-name fees for many mailers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile-based matching methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a profile of title words, authors, and publications that characterize the target interest and match that profile against a database to retrieve appropriate names and addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively test and refine profiles; the example method used for ASCA/Automatic Citation Alert demonstrates building profiles from literature and using automated searches to generate mailing lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of list specificity to product type
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly specialized products and informational mailings require highly selective lists (e.g., only practicing researchers in a tiny discipline), while general-purpose mailings can use less specific lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the selectivity of the list to the specificity of the offering—overly broad lists waste resources for niche products; overly narrow lists miss opportunities for broader offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of hard-to-find individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication-based and specialized lists can capture individuals not affiliated with academic or professional institutions (e.g., researchers in industry) who are omitted from membership lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publication/activity-based compilations to reach practitioners who do not appear in standard institutional directories or membership rosters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to detect and prevent fictitious/list-abuse entries
rubrics_metrics.description: To detect unauthorized or fictitious names used for monitoring or illicit purposes, list managers include measures (e.g., fictitious names) and monitor usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include integrity checks and monitoring on each list; remove or block users detected to be misusing list data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to localize by country and market restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems should allow preselection by country to avoid sending mail to locations where no market exists or where currency/other factors make mailing inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide country-level filters and consider market/currency and legal/regulatory issues before including international addresses in a campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of recipient attitudes and preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys and preference services (e.g., DMMA Mail Preference Service) reveal that many recipients prefer receiving some direct mail; attitudes vary (helpful vs annoying).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey data and preference registries to inform mailing frequency, content, and opt-in/opt-out practices; respect requests for removal and use preference services to reduce complaints.
